deep.reconstruction:
The page continues a table of quadratic residues for primes, which runs across fol. 6r, 6v and 7r. For each prime p the left margin carries a sign above the number: '+' if p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and '−' if p ≡ 3 (mod 4). This sign is the value of the Legendre symbol (−1/p). After the prime comes a second sign. For p ≡ 1 mod 4 it is '∓': residues are symmetric under a ↦ p−a, so only the residues a ≤ (p−1)/2 are written, and ±a are both meant. For p ≡ 3 mod 4 it is '+', and all residues a in 1..p−1 are written. In modern terms, each row is {a : 1 ≤ a ≤ N, (a/p) = 1}, with N = (p−1)/2 or p−1. Each list should therefore have (p−1)/4 entries (if p ≡ 1 mod 4) or (p−1)/2 entries (if p ≡ 3 mod 4).

Top block (struck '10#', then '1.(4)'): this continues the residue list of p = 383 from fol. 6r, from 216 to 378. The marginal '256.258' at the top is an insertion into the gap 252–260; these are exactly the two residues of 383 in 253–259.

In line 2, the entries 267, 269, 271, 275 are struck and replaced by 265, 266, 268, 272, 274, 276, 278 written above. My Legendre-symbol computations confirm that 267 = 3·89, 269, 271 and 275 = 25·11 are non-residues mod 383, while 265, 266, 268, 272, 274, 276, 278 are residues. The list correctly ends at 378 = −5: (5/383) = −1 and (−1/383) = −1. The values 379–382 (= −4, −3, −2, −1) are non-residues.

The remaining rows are:
- p = 389 (≡ 5 mod 8, so 2 is a non-residue; 3 is a non-residue): residues 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, … up to 194. The last entries are 183, 184, 187, 193. Here 184 was struck at the line end and rewritten above. The tally scribble at the end is a deletion.
- p = 397 (≡ 5 mod 8): residues 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, … ≤ 198. Insertions 92 and 163 are correct residues.
- p = 401 (≡ 1 mod 8, so 2 is a residue; 3 is a non-residue): residues 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, … ≤ 200.
- p = 409 (≡ 1 mod 8): residues 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, … ≤ 204. Note that 7 is absent, which is correct since (409/7) = (3/7) = −1.
- p = 419 (≡ 3 mod 8, sign '−', so the full list to 418 is given): residues 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, … , 417.

Corrections in the 419 row:
- Between 235 and 243 the struck block is replaced by 236, 237, 238, 240. I verified these are the only residues in 236–242.
- The superscript '5' turns the next entry into 245. Between 248 and 251 the tally is a deletion; 249 and 250 are non-residues.
- '4 25 26' above gives 324, 325, 326.
- The last line reads 388, 389, 393, 395, then a struck tally. The final residues 400, 401, 402, 405, 408, 409, 411, 413, 417 are written above. 417 = −2 is a residue, because (−1/419) = (2/419) = −1.

The method is presumably sieving by multiplicativity, or listing squares mod p, with later spot-corrections. Its purpose is a working table of quadratic residues and non-residues for primes in roughly the 350–440 range, continuing the tables of the preceding and following pages. Such tables are of the kind Gauss used for reciprocity, class-number and factoring work.
errors: No uncorrected errors found in the entries I spot-checked by Legendre-symbol computation. These include the ends of the 383, 389 and 419 lists, all corrected or inserted entries, and the starts of all rows.

The visible corrections are Gauss's own fixes of earlier slips. In the 383 row, 267, 269, 271, 275 (non-residues) had been entered and 265, 266, 268, 272, 274, 276, 278 omitted. In the 383 row, 256 and 258 were omitted. In the 419 row, a block near 236–250 and the entries 324–326 were miswritten. Gauss's corrections are right in every case I checked.

results.what: Tables of quadratic residues mod p for p = 383 (continued), 389, 397, 401, 409, 419. Only half-lists are given for p ≡ 1 mod 4, using (−1/p) = 1. Each prime is marked with the sign of (−1/p).
results.modern_name: Quadratic residue table / Legendre symbol values
results.usually_credited_to: Residue tables are classical (Euler, Legendre); Gauss published a residue table in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Table II.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational table of quadratic residues. Gauss is well known to have computed extensive residue and number-theoretic tables, some printed in the Werke. The only interest is archival detail: the extent of the table and the corrections.
